AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: To review the impact of antibiotic allergy and resistance in older women with recurrent urinary tract infections (RUTIs) as determinants for a suitable oral antibiotic treatment choice.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: A prospectively maintained database of women 65 years old and older with documented RUTIs (≥3 UTI/year) and trigonitis on cystoscopy was reviewed. Demographic data, known drug allergies, renal function, antibiotic susceptibility of most recent urine culture, allergy and/or resistance to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), fluoroquinolones, and nitrofurantoin were obtained.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: From 2006-2014, 86 women with RUTIs met study crtieria. Mean age was 77.9±7.8 with 94% being Caucasian. An eGFR >30mL/min was noted in 94%. The percentage of women allergic, resistant, or both allergic and resistant to TMP-SMX was 33%, 29%, and 15%, to fluoroquinolones was 14%, 34%, and 8.1%, or nitrofurantoin was 16%, 14%, and 5% respectively. Twenty-eight percent (24/86) of women who were allergic and/or resistant to TMP-SMX and fluoroquinolones were sensitive to nitrofurantoin. Twenty percent (17/86) were allergic and/or resistant to all three antibiotics. Women who were allergic or resistant to TMP-SMX had a significantly higher number of other antibiotic resistances compared to women sensitive to TMP-SMX (4.9±3.6 versus 2.1±2.3; p < 0.0001). Similarly, women with fluoroquinolone allergy or resistance had significantly more antibiotic resistances than those who were fluoroquinolone sensitive (5.8±3.5 versus 2.3±2.5; p < 0.0001).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Due to allergy and/or antibiotic resistance, several first-line antibiotics are not available for many older women with RUTIs. In nearly a third of women, nitrofurantoin was the only viable alternative.
